entry.title: Version 1.3.0: teleported views always know where they are 🧭
entry.summary: react-native-teleport 1.3.0 is on its way. This release rewrites how Fabric measures teleported content: instead of keeping a pre-calculated offset in sync with the screen, a teleported Portal now looks up the position of its host directly in the shadow tree.
entry.content:
react-native-teleport 1.3.0 is on its way. This release rewrites how Fabric measures teleported content: instead of keeping a pre-calculated offset in sync with the screen, a teleported Portal now looks up the position of its host directly in the shadow tree.

The result: measure() and Pressable keep working after you scroll, and a whole class of "stale position" bugs is gone for good!

🗺️ One view, two addresses​

When you render something through a Portal, it lives in two places at once:

  • in the React tree (and in Fabric's shadow tree, which mirrors it) it's still a child of the Portal. This is what keeps context, state and props working;
  • on the screen (the native view hierarchy) it's a child of the PortalHost. This is where it's actually drawn.

Most of the time nobody cares about this difference. But sometimes React Native asks: "where exactly on the screen is this view?". measure() asks it, and Pressable asks it all the time while you hold your finger on a button: if the finger moves too far away from the button, the press gets cancelled.

To answer this question Fabric walks up the shadow tree and adds up the positions of all parents. And in the shadow tree our button still sits inside the Portal, at its old place. So without any help Fabric points at the wrong spot.

🏠 The old way: "go to my old house and walk 3 blocks"​

Since 1.1.10 (#150) we helped Fabric with a correction. The native side measured where the host and the source are on the screen and stored the difference between them (host − source) as an offset in the portal state. Fabric then calculated the position as:

position = Portal (shadow tree) + offset (native)

Think of it as directions like "go to my old house, then walk 3 blocks east". It works perfectly - as long as the old house doesn't move.

But it can! Declare a Portal inside a ScrollView and scroll it: the first part of the formula changes (Fabric knows about the scroll), while the second part stays the same (scrolling doesn't trigger any layout callback on the native side, so nobody recalculates the "3 blocks"). Now the answer is off by exactly the scroll distance, and Pressable cancels your press as soon as the finger moves a little (#220):

1.2.5: the measured position is off by the scroll distance (240), the second press is cancelled1.3.0: the measured position matches the actual one, the press is counted

The two halves of the formula come from two different worlds that get updated at different moments. We had already fixed another case where these two parts drifted apart (#172), and every such fix meant one more native hook whose only job was to keep two numbers in sync. Recalculating the offset on every frame would have worked too, but then every teleported view would cost you work on every frame, even when nothing moves.

🧭 The new way: just ask where the host is​

In 1.3.0 we stopped patching the formula and removed the source from it entirely.

A teleported Portal is now marked as a root node in the shadow tree (the RootNodeKind trait). This is the same trick React Native uses for <Modal> and react-native-screens uses for FullWindowOverlay - both have the same "lives here, drawn there" problem. When Fabric measures a view and reaches such a node, it stops walking up.

At that point the Portal tells Fabric where to continue from: the position of the host, read from the same revision of the shadow tree that is being measured.

position = host (shadow tree)

Back to the analogy: instead of "old house + 3 blocks" you now hand out the real address. Scroll the source, scroll the host, transform, rotate, re-layout - the answer is calculated at the moment of the question, from the data Fabric already has.

✨ Why it's better​

  • Nothing can get stale. There is no cached offset anymore, so there is nothing to keep in sync. Scrolling the source and scrolling the host are fixed by the same change.
  • Nothing runs per frame. The position is calculated only when somebody asks for it.
  • Less native code. The native side now reports only which host the children are mounted into and its size. The screen offset calculations and the layout and attachment hooks on iOS and Android are gone.
  • One source of truth. Layout, transforms and scroll offsets of the host's ancestors are taken exactly as Fabric knows them. A new way of moving something on the screen is covered automatically, instead of waiting for its own bug report and its own fix.

On top of that, 1.3.0 removes a one-frame flash on Android when a Portal switches to another host (#228): the Portal now takes the size of the new host in the same commit that changes hostName, instead of drawing one frame with the layout of the previous host.

📦 Why 1.3.0 and not 1.2.6?​

There are no API changes - your code stays exactly the same. But the way the library is linked into React Native has changed:

  • to read the shadow tree the library now uses Fabric's UIManager (through ShadowTreeRevisionProvider) and RuntimeScheduler. Everything it needs is available starting from React Native 0.78, so this is the new minimum supported version;
  • on iOS the library depends on more React Native pods. With use_frameworks! and React Native built from source, the podspec now declares React-runtimescheduler, React-performancetimeline and (up to React Native 0.81) React-jsinspectortracing for you.

Since this can affect your build, it deserves a minor version rather than a patch that you might pull in without noticing.

🚀 Upgrading​

yarn add react-native-teleport@1.3.0
cd ios && pod install
React-native < 0.78

If you are on React Native older than 0.78 - stay on 1.2.x until you upgrade React Native.

If you notice a wrong position, a cancelled press or a build issue after upgrading, please open an issue with your React Native version and a reproduction.

entry.title: What's coming in 1.2.0: smoother teleportation on Android 🚀
entry.summary: react-native-teleport 1.2.0 is just around the corner. This release focuses on one major improvement: a reworked reparenting mechanism on Android.
entry.content:
react-native-teleport 1.2.0 is just around the corner. This release focuses on one major improvement: a reworked reparenting mechanism on Android.

With the new fast path, you should see in most cases no empty frames while teleporting views. The difference is especially noticeable for surface-backed content such as videos and maps.

⬜ Why did empty frames appear?​

Teleport moves an existing native view between parents without remounting the React component. On Android, that move previously used the regular removeView() and addView() APIs.

Although the same React component and native view were preserved, Android temporarily detached the view from the window. For content backed by a SurfaceView or TextureView, that could disconnect or recreate the rendering surface. While Android waited for the next frame, the background underneath became visible as a black, white, or otherwise empty flash.

This was easier to spot on older devices, but it could also happen intermittently on newer versions of Android.

🚀 A faster reparenting path​

In 1.2.0, Teleport can move an already attached view using Android's lightweight detachViewFromParent() and attachViewToParent() APIs.

The view is removed from one parent's child list and inserted into the other synchronously, without leaving the Android window. This keeps its rendering resources alive and lets the compositor continue displaying the previously submitted frame throughout the move.

In practice, teleporting videos, maps, and other surface-backed views should now feel much more seamless.

Video is flickering while teleportingVideo gets teleported without flickering

🛡️ Safe by default​

The fast path is used only when Teleport can safely preserve the view's window attachment - for example, when both parents belong to the same Android window and no active focus or layout transition requires the full detach lifecycle.

When those conditions are not met, Teleport automatically falls back to the existing removeView() and addView() behavior. There is no new API or configuration to adopt: the optimization happens internally.

🧪 Tested against empty frames​

Alongside the new mechanism, we added an end-to-end regression test that records a video teleportation and checks the result for empty frames. This gives us a way to catch the original visual glitch automatically before it reaches another release.

The fast path has also been tested with video and map content across Android API levels 28, 31, and 36.

✨ Upgrading​

There are no breaking API changes in 1.2.0. Upgrade as usual:

yarn add react-native-teleport@1.2.0

That's it - existing teleports will automatically use the new Android fast path whenever it is safe to do so.

If you still notice an empty frame after upgrading, please open an issue with your device, Android version, and the type of view being teleported.

entry.title: Illusion of portals in React Native 🛸
entry.summary: Ever wondered what really happens when you render something through a portal in React Native?
entry.content:
Ever wondered what really happens when you render something through a portal in React Native?

In my talk The Illusion of Portals in React Native at App.js Conf, we look beyond the familiar Portal API to understand how different implementations actually work, how they affect the React tree, and what a true portal should look like internally — from the illusion created at the React layer to native portals, view re-parenting, and the new possibilities they unlock.

Step through the portal and join me for the ride!

entry.title: Meet teleport!
entry.summary: I'm excited to announce the first stable release of react-native-teleport! 🎉
entry.content:
I'm excited to announce the first stable release of react-native-teleport! 🎉

After extensive development, community feedback and integrating the lib into many prod apps, we've reached a big milestone: a production-ready portal solution that brings true native portals to react-native — something the framework has been missing for years.

What is react-native-teleport?​

react-native-teleport solves a fundamental problem in React Native development: it brings missing Portal component to react-native.

Historically, developers had to use JS based solutions to render modals, tooltips, overlays, and other components that need to visually appear in a different part of your UI tree. While they work, they have significant limitation: they physically render components in a different part of React tree, breaking context and bringing other related problems.

The react-native-teleport solves this problem by moving rendering of components in the native layer. This library provides a declarative API, doesn't rely on internal React implementation details, and works identically on iOS, Android, and Web.

Not only Portal​

As you may noticed from the library title this library is not only a portal solution. It also provides a re-parenting pattern that allows you to move existing components without unmounting or remounting them.

With that technique you can build advanced and seamless transitions, implement shared-element-style transitions between screens, and more.

For example you can implement photos app transitions like this without flickering, white/black screens, jumps and other distracting things:


The great thing is that view is not re-created or destroyed when it's moved between different parents. This mean you can use this lib for stateful components, like Video/Lottie etc. and you can easily replicate patterns that you've seen in many well-known apps, for example you can re-build Instagram-like reels transition:


Not only about transitions and rendering outside​

Traditionally, React has three operations in its reconciliation mechanism: create, update, and destroy. When you move a component from one parent to another in the React tree, it gets destroyed and recreated.

But effectively react-native-teleport unlocks a new dimension and introduces a fourth operation: move. This is a game-changer because it allows you to:

Pre-render Components Offscreen​

You can render expensive components off-screen and move them into view only when needed. This is particularly useful for complex overlays, modals, or bottom sheets that require significant setup time.

// Pre-render the editor off-screen
<Portal hostName={used ? "editor" : undefined}>
  <ExpensiveRichTextEditor />
</Portal>

// Later, when user triggers an action, simply move it into view
// No re-rendering, no state loss, just a native view reposition

Re-use Views Between Screens​

One of the most powerful patterns enabled by the "move" operation is view reuse across navigation transitions. You can render the same component instance on multiple screens and seamlessly move it as users navigate.

Imagine you have the same component rendered twice on two different screens. If it's heavy for rendering a typical path is to dig into performance bottlenecks, fixing them etc. But with react-native-teleport you can simply move the component between screens 🤯

And more​

I'm still exploring of what can be done with this library. Things that I discovered helped to build flicker free transitions while moving heavy views and helped to optimize performance from the angle that I never thought about (just re-using the view without re-creating it).

But I continue to explore what other patterns and use cases can be enabled with this library. I'm also looking for feedback from the community and I'm open to suggestions and ideas.

What's Next?​

I have exciting plans for future releases:

  • 🪞 Mirror support for advanced mirroring patterns
  • 🚀 Performance optimizations
  • 🤓 Additional platform support
  • 🙌 Community-driven features based on feedback

Thank You​

This milestone wouldn't be possible without the incredible react-native community. Thank you to everyone who tested, provided feedback, reported issues, and contributed to making react-native-teleport better.

If you find this library useful, please consider:

  • ⭐ Starring on GitHub
  • 📢 Sharing with the community
  • 🐛 Reporting issues and providing feedback
  • 🤝 Contributing improvements
